affiliations: Neuroscience, Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, Florida
s1-01.keywords: Alzheimer’s disease, extracellular vesicles, microglia, microtubule-associated protein tau, mitochondria

p: Microglia play a central role in the neuroinflammatory processes underlying Alzheimer’s disease (AD), potentially accelerating disease progression through the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines and secretion of extracellular vesicles (EVs). Thus, targeting molecules driving microglial EV secretion represents a promising strategy to halt tau pathology progression. P2RX7 is an interesting target due to its high expression in microglia in AD and regulation of EV secretion. We investigated the role of P2rx7 deficiency in tau pathology, EV secretion and microglia in PS19 mouse model of tauopathy.

PS19:P2rx7KO mice (9-10 months old) were evaluated using fear conditioning test and their brain sections were assessed for brain atrophy (volumetric analysis) and tau pathology (immunostaining for AT8 and Alz50). Bulk and single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) were performed on brain tissue. To visualize microglial EV secretion in vivo, P2rx7KO mice were intracranially injected with viral vectors expressing P301L-tau in neurons and mEmerald-CD9 in microglia. Brain-derived EVs were isolated and analyzed via mass spectrometry, then injected into wild-type (WT) mice to assess microglial responses by cell sorting and RNA-seq. Primary cultured neurons and microglia were used to confirm EV and P2rx7 function.

PS19:P2rx7KO mice showed improved contextual and cued fear memory, reduced brain atrophy, and significantly decreased synaptic loss and tau pathology compared to age-matched PS19 mice. We identified a P2rx7-dependent gene module enriched in microglial and EV genes associated with tau pathology. scRNA-seq revealed a P2rx7-dependent microglial shift toward a pro-inflammatory phenotype with upregulated EV gene expression in PS19 mice, consisting with reduced microglial EV secretion observed in P2rx7-deficient mice expressing P301L-tau. EV proteome demonstrates that P2RX7 increases loading of tau and mitochondrial proteins into PS19 brain-derived EVs, enriched with mtDNA. Importantly, EVs secreted from mitochondrially stressed cells activate cytosolic DNA-sensing and interferon signaling in recipient microglia, contributing to inflammatory response.

We discovered a new mechanism associated with propagation of inflammatory response through EV-containing mitochondrial cargo in tauopathy. This microglial P2RX7–EV axis contributes to tau-associated neurodegeneration and presents a potential therapeutic target for mitigating AD progression.

affiliations: Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, Florida
s1-02.keywords: GEMMs, mouse model, Kras, pancreatic cancer, Kras-driven cancer

p: Genetically engineered mouse models (GEMMs) harboring conditional mutant Kras alleles, such as LSL-KrasG12D, have been widely used to investigate tumorigenesis and therapeutic responses. However, the design of these alleles has an intrinsic limitation: in non-recombined tissues, the targeted allele blocks WT Kras expression, resulting in functional Kras heterozygosity, which may alter normal Kras function in multiple biological systems, including the immune system. Furthermore, homozygosity for the LSL-KrasG12D allele eliminates WT Kras expression, resulting in embryonic lethality and thereby increasing breeding time, cost, and animal use. To overcome these limitations, we aimed to develop a novel mouse model in which endogenous WT Kras expression is preserved prior to Cre-mediated recombination and subsequently switches to oncogenic KrasG12D expression.

We used the FLEx system with a KrasFLEx-G12D donor construct containing WT Kras exon 1 and an inverted mutant KrasG12D exon 1 flanked by nested, oppositely oriented loxP and lox2272 sites. These incompatible lox sites enable Cre-mediated inversion and stable switching between WT Kras and oncogenic KrasG12D expression. The construct was targeted to the endogenous Kras locus using CRISPR-Cas9 in C57BL/6J mice. Founder mice were screened for targeted integration by PCR-based genotyping. Functional activation of the KrasFLEx-G12D allele was evaluated by crossing these mice with pancreas-specific Pdx1-Cre mice. Mutant KrasG12D expression was detected by RT-PCR and Western blotting using a G12D-specific Kras antibody.

Twenty F0 candidate pups were obtained, of which five (25%) demonstrated correct homology-directed repair (HDR)-mediated integration at the endogenous Kras locus by PCR. In KrasFLEx-G12D; Pdx1-Cre compound mice, mutant KrasG12D mRNA and protein were detected in the pancreas but not in WT or KrasFLEx-G12D littermate controls. Unlike the LSL-KrasG12D mice, the KrasFLEx-G12D mice can be bred to homozygosity, consistent with preservation of WT Kras expression.

We developed a novel KrasFLEx-G12D mouse model that preserves endogenous WT Kras expression prior to Cre activation and subsequently switches to oncogenic KrasG12D expression, providing a more physiologically relevant model with improved breeding efficiency and reduced animal use for Kras-driven cancer research.

affiliations: Neuroscience, Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, Florida

p: Aging is marked by aberrant neuroinflammation driven by microglia and astrocytes, yet how apolipoprotein E (APOE) genotype, the strongest genetic modifier of longevity and Alzheimer’s disease, influence glial aging remains unclear.

We used young (3 months) and aged (24 months) humanized APOE2, APOE3, and APOE4 mice to profile transcriptomic changes in microglia and astrocytes using single-cell RNA sequencing (n = 4 mice/genotype/age). In parallel, CD11b⁺ microglia and ACSA2⁺ astrocytes were sequentially isolated from an independent cohort (n = 6 mice per/genotype/age) for proteomic analysis to assess age-related translational changes. Key findings were validated using immunostaining and electron microscopy in additional independent cohorts.

Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed the most transcriptional alterations in APOE2 across both glial types. In contrast, proteomic analyses showed the fewest changes in APOE2 and the most in APOE4, with immune-related pathways commonly altered. Validation confirmed that age-related glial activation was enriched in white matter, where aged APOE2 mice exhibited preserved myelin homeostasis, while APOE3 and APOE4 mice showed impaired myelin integrity. Aging also led to an accumulation of CD8⁺ T cells in white matter, likely driven by activated glia rather than APOE genotype.
These findings highlight roles for APOE and aging in regulating glial activation, myelin integrity, and immune responses.

affiliations: Division of Vascular and Endovascular Surgery, Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, Florida
s1-04.keywords: Carotid artery stenosis, symptomatic carotid disease, carotid endarterectomy, carotid artery stenting, revascularization timing.

p: Early intervention for symptomatic carotid artery disease (CAD) may benefit patients, yet the optimal timing window is debated. This study evaluated the impact of timing of revascularization on perioperative and long-term outcomes.

We reviewed 821 carotid revascularization procedures for CAD from 2016-2026. Procedures were stratified by into urgent (0–2 days), early (3–14 days), and delayed (≥15 days) groups. Endpoints included 30-day and long-term mortality, ipsilateral stroke, transient ischemic attack (TIA), myocardial infarction (MI), and a composite of these events, plus restenosis and reintervention. Cox regressions identified independent predictors of the outcomes. Sensitivity analyses adjusted for factors related to adjunct procedures at the time of initial neurovascular event presentation.

The cohort's median age was 74.2 years; the majority were males (69.4%). High rates of hypertension (86.1%), hyperlipidemia (84.4%), and coronary artery disease (35.6%) were observed. The most common presentation was stroke (48.4%), followed by TIA (31.8%) and amaurosis fugax (19.9%). The 30-day composite outcome of stroke, TIA, MI, or death was significantly lower in the early group (2.8%) compared to delayed (4.0%) and urgent (8.0%) groups (P=0.03). Thirty-day mortality was higher in the urgent group (2.9%) than in the early (0.3%) and delayed (0.3%) groups (P=0.01). On Cox regression, urgent timing (HR 2.50; P=0.044) and absent preoperative antithrombotic therapy (HR 3.75; P=0.006) were independent predictors of the 30-day composite outcome. At a median follow-up of 2.8 years, long-term MI was more frequent in the early group (4.7%) than in the urgent (1.5%) and delayed (1.6%) groups (P=0.03). Restenosis was highest in the urgent group (9.5%), followed by delayed (5.3%) and early groups (3.9%; P=0.05). Reintervention followed the same pattern (urgent 6.6% vs. delayed 3.1% vs. early 1.1%; P<0.01). On Cox regression, both urgent (HR 4.13; P=0.018) and delayed timing (HR 5.63; P=0.003) were independently associated with higher reintervention risk compared to early revascularization.

Early carotid revascularization have most favorable perioperative and long-term outcomes. Urgent revascularization carries significantly higher perioperative risk, while delayed intervention beyond 14 days reduces the potential preventive benefit of timely revascularization and is associated with higher long-term reintervention rates.

s1-05.keywords: mesenchymal stem cells, chronic kidney disease, senescence, inflammation

p: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is the leading cause of kidney failure worldwide, with no curative therapies. Cellular senescence and inflammation contribute to DKD pathogenesis. Mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC)-based therapies reduce inflammation and fibrosis in preclinical DKD models via paracrine mediated repair mechanisms; however, their interactions with contemporary DKD pharmacotherapies remain poorly understood.

We hypothesized that combining MSC-conditioned media (MSC-CM) with canagliflozin, a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor (SGLT2i), and/or tirzepatide, a dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist, would enhance protection against DKD-associated tubular injury.

Human proximal tubular epithelial (HK-2) cells were exposed to high glucose (30 mM) and TGF-β (5 ng/mL) for 6 hours, followed by 18 hours of MSC-CM alone or combined with canagliflozin, tirzepatide, or both. Control, injury, and MSC media-control groups were included. Gene expression was assessed by qPCR for INHBA, TNC, CDKN1A/p21, CDKN2A/p16, IL6, SIRT1, and KL.

Injury markedly increased activin A (INHBA) expression, which was reduced with addition of MSC-CM, but no further reduction when combined with canagliflozin and/or tirzepatide. Geroprotective marker Klotho (KL) expression decreased with injury and remained reduced following MSC-CM treatment. In contrast, addition of tirzepatide and/or canagliflozin to MSC-CM significantly increased KL above healthy controls, suggesting enhanced geroprotective signaling. Senescence and inflammation markers (CDKN1A/p21, CDKN2A/p16, IL6), extracellular matrix remodeling marker (TNC) and geroprotective (SIRT1) markers were not consistently modulated between treatment groups (vs. controls). These findings suggest MSC-CM suppresses the injury-associated INHBA response whereas pharmacologic additions provide a distinct benefit to KL expression, showing potential for complementary pathways of tubular repair.

To assess clinical relevance, in vitro responses will be compared with outcomes from adults with CKD receiving MSC therapy through the Mayo Clinic Florida Regenerative Nephrology Compassionate Use Program, stratified by concurrent SGLT2i and incretin-based (GLP-1) therapy, to determine how standard of care pharmacotherapies modify MSC therapeutic responses.

affiliations: Laboratory Medicine and Pathology, Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, Florida

p: Gliomas bearing IDH1/2 mutations (IDHmut) represent a unique subtype of this disease that progresses from low- to high-grade lesions. Despite their relatively positive prognosis compared to IDH1/2 wildtype glioblastomas, these brain tumors are nonetheless invariably fatal. New targeted therapies that inhibit IDHmut enzyme function have emerged for low-grade gliomas, but these therapies have not yet proven to be effective in high-grade counterparts.

Five high-grade IDHmut glioma cultures were treated with the IDHmut inhibitor vorasidenib using short-term (5 days) and long-term (4 months) treatment. For long-term treatments, longitudinal sample acquisition occurred every month. Cytotoxicity (trypan blue) and proliferation (EdU) assays were conducted at each timepoint, in addition to acquisition of flash-frozen cell pellets for multi-dimensional transcriptomic, DNA methylation, and proteomic analyses.

Short-term (5 day) dose-response analysis of vorasidenib between 0-1 µM showed no effect on cytotoxicity or cell proliferation in our IDHmut glioma cultures as determined by Countess cell growth and cytotoxicity assays. ELISAs showed that vorasidenib elicited maximum inhibition of D2HG production in all our cell cultures at a concentration as low as 10 nM, and that this inhibition extended through our entire 4-month treatment period. Interestingly, two different IDHmut glioma cultures (TS603, MGG152) displayed accelerated growth after 2-3 months of treatment with vorasidenib, supporting a delayed epigenetic mechanism of growth activation. Multi-dimensional transcriptomic, DNA methylation, and proteomic analyses are ongoing.

Considering that IDHmut create epigenomic DNA hypermethylation (G-CIMP high) through production of the oncometabolite D2HG, and that this hypermethylation is partially lost due to reduced D2HG levels during malignant tumor progression (G-CIMP low), we hypothesize that IDHmut enzyme inhibition imposes undesirable tumor growth activation in a subset of these patients. Future goals will be to correlate this work with clinical samples from vorasidenib-treated patients to identify pre- and post-treatment biomarkers that may be able to predict negative treatment response in patients receiving IDHmut inhibitors.

affiliations: Pain Medicine Department, Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, Florida
s1-07.keywords: Childhood Trauma, Interdisciplinary Pain Rehabilitation, Health-Related Quality of Life, Psychological Distress, Trauma-Informed Care

p: Chronic pain is influenced by biological, psychological, and social factors, including adverse childhood experiences (ACEs). Although higher ACE exposure is associated with greater psychological distress and poorer functioning, its impact on outcomes after interdisciplinary pain rehabilitation is not well understood. This study examined whether ACE burden affected treatment response and clinically meaningful improvement following participation in an interdisciplinary pain rehabilitation program.

This retrospective cohort study included 985 adults with chronic pain who completed a 2-week interdisciplinary Pain Rehabilitation Center program at Mayo Clinic Florida between January 2022 and February 2025 (IRB #24-013423). Participants were categorized into high (≥3) and low (≤2) ACE groups. Outcomes included depressive symptoms (CES-D), pain catastrophizing (PCS), and health-related quality of life (SF-36), assessed at admission and discharge. Clinically meaningful improvement was defined using established MCID thresholds. Multivariable regression and mediation analyses were performed.

Participants with high ACE exposure had significantly worse baseline psychological and functional status. Despite this, both groups demonstrated significant improvements across all outcomes, with mean changes meeting or exceeding MCID thresholds. Compared with the low-ACE group, high-ACE participants experienced greater reductions in depressive symptoms (−13.4 vs. −10.7, p<0.001) and pain catastrophizing (−11.5 vs. −9.7, p=0.02), as well as greater improvement in physical functioning (p=0.006). High ACE status independently predicted clinically meaningful improvement in depression (OR 1.82, 95% CI 1.39-2.39, p<0.001). Reductions in pain catastrophizing partially mediated improvements in depressive symptoms.

Individuals with greater childhood adversity entered treatment with more severe impairment but achieved comparable or better outcomes following interdisciplinary pain rehabilitation. Trauma exposure should not be considered a barrier to rehabilitation success. Trauma-informed, biopsychosocial interventions may further enhance outcomes in chronic pain care.

affiliations: Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, Florida
s1-08.keywords: Spinal cord injury; Wheelchair propulsion; Arthritis; Pain; Musculoskeletal Health

p: Manual wheelchair propulsion places substantial mechanical demands on the upper extremities, particularly the shoulder complex. However, existing evidence has focused primarily on shoulder-specific symptoms or pathology, and it remains unclear whether propulsion type is associated with broader musculoskeletal and pain outcomes. We compared self-reported arthritis, pain severity, and pain interference across manual wheelchair users, power/power-assist users, and non-wheelchair users with traumatic spinal cord injury.

We conducted a retrospective, cross-sectional secondary analysis of the National Spinal Cord Injury Statistical Center Spinal Cord Injury Model Systems Public Use Database. The sample included 10,521 unique adults who completed a follow-up interview from 2017 through 2021. Arthritis prevalence was compared using chi-square tests, and pain severity and interference using Kruskal-Wallis tests. Multivariable logistic, linear, and ordinal logistic regression evaluated associations after adjustment for age, sex, years since injury, neurologic level, and ASIA Impairment Scale grade.

The sample included 4,104 manual users, 3,094 power/power-assist users, and 3,323 non-users. Arthritis prevalence was 22.7%, 29.4%, and 37.6%, respectively (P<.001). Unadjusted pain severity did not differ across groups (P=.53), whereas pain interference was higher among non-users than both wheelchair-using groups (P<.001). After adjustment, manual users had lower odds of arthritis than non-users (aOR, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.65–0.87; P<.001). Compared with manual users, non-users had higher pain severity (b=0.26; 95% CI, 0.09–0.44; P=.004) and pain interference (aOR, 1.26; 95% CI, 1.12–1.41; P<.001). Power/power-assist users also had higher pain severity (b=0.19; 95% CI, 0.03–0.35; P=.018), pain interference (aOR, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.00–1.22; P=.043), and odds of arthritis (aOR, 1.35; 95% CI, 1.18–1.54; P<.001) than manual users.

Manual wheelchair users had the lowest arthritis prevalence and, after adjustment, the lowest pain severity and pain interference, the inverse of what a shoulder-overuse hypothesis would predict. Because the outcomes were not joint-specific, these findings do not refute shoulder-specific risk from manual propulsion. Rather, manual propulsion may mark greater functional independence and activity. Residual confounding, selection, reverse causation, and the cross-sectional design preclude causal interpretation.

affiliations: Department of Neurology, Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, Florida
s1-09.keywords: cerebral amyloid angiopathy, seizures, epilepsy, cognitive decline, intracerebral hemorrhage

p: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) is an amyloid mediated cortical and leptomeningeal small-vessel disease that commonly presents with lobar intracerebral hemorrhage, cognitive impairment, and transient neurological symptoms. Epilepsy occurs in 20-33% of patients with CAA, but their association with cognitive function and survival remains incompletely defined.

We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Mayo Clinic Platform, which contains multi-institutional de-identified longitudinal electronic health records. Adult patients (≥18 years) with CAA were identified using ICD-10 code I68.0 and natural language processing of clinical notes including Boston criteria 2.0. Epilepsy was defined per ILAE criteria with ICD-10 codes and documentation in clinical notes, and cognitive dysfunction diagnosis was confirmed using patient history. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed at the date of CAA diagnosis. Time-to-event outcomes were estimated using Kaplan-Meier methods and Cox proportional hazards regression for 60 months follow-up.

Among the 2,717 patients with CAA (mean age 74.5 years), 733 patients (27.0%) had epilepsy. 673 propensity score–matched pairs were included in the final analysis. Epilepsy was associated with a higher risk of cognitive dysfunction (HR 1.34, 95% CI 1.13-1.60). No statistically significant difference was noted in all-cause mortality between cohorts (HR 1.07, 95% CI 0.86-1.33).

Epilepsy in patients with CAA was associated with higher risk of cognitive decline. There was no difference in all-cause mortality, but the confidence interval does not exclude a clinically meaningful effect in either direction. These findings highlight patients with epilepsy as a subgroup of CAA cases with increased risk for cognitive decline. Prospective studies with validated cognitive assessments are needed to confirm this association.

affiliations: Neurosurgery, Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, Florida
s1-10.keywords: Glioblastoma; Tumor microenvironment; Invasion; Extracellular Matrix; Spatial Transcriptomics; Multiomics

p: Glioblastoma (GBM) recurs from invasive cells at the infiltrated margin, the region left behind after surgery and the primary site of recurrence, yet clinical decision-making relies almost entirely on tissue from the resected core. We generated a paired single-cell spatial multi-omic atlas of matched tumor core and margin specimens (20 specimens, 10 newly diagnosed IDH-wild-type GBM patients), integrating Xenium 5,000-plex spatial transcriptomics with CosMx 64-plex spatial proteomics registered to neuropathologist-annotated histology. The atlas resolves the complete GBM ecosystem across four compartments: 7 malignant states and 16 immune, 10 brain-resident, and 7 vascular-stromal populations organized into 10 spatial niches. Tumor cores were dominated by MES-/AC-like malignant cells, monocyte-derived TAMs, and reactive vascular stroma, whereas margins shifted toward OPC-/NPC-like states embedded among neurons, oligodendrocytes, and homeostatic microglia. Applying orthogonal invasion signatures, we identified two biologically separable invasion programs that classify different tumor cells: mesenchymal invasion, predominant in the core and declining toward the margin, and neurodevelopmental invasion, sustained at the margin with marked inter-patient variability. Two niches were selectively permissive to invasion: the immune-active OPC-interface and proliferative-progenitor niches. Clinically, total margin invasion burden, irrespective of program, predicted early progression: margin invasion correlated inversely with progression-free survival (Spearman ρ = −0.68, p = 0.045), and patients above a 30% threshold progressed within ~3 months versus later progression in all patients below it (median PFS 1.2 vs 8.4 months; log-rank p = 0.0072), while core invasion showed no association (p = 0.36). The effect remained stable after individual adjustment for MGMT methylation, age, extent of resection, KPS, multifocality, and ventricular contact (HR 1.2–1.4 per 10 percentage points), none of which was itself prognostic. Margin invasion burden at diagnosis is a candidate biomarker to prioritize patients for early trial enrollment and intensified imaging surveillance, and each invasion program constitutes a regionally distinct therapeutic target for the cells that seed recurrence.

affiliations: Neurosciences, Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, Florida

p: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder featuring a pathological hallmark of neurofibrillary tangles composed of abnormally phosphorylated tau, which significantly contribute to synaptic degradation and cognitive dysfunction. Tau tubulin kinase-1 (TTBK1) is a brain-specific serine/threonine and tyrosine kinase implicated in tau pathology, evidenced by reports of high neuronal expression in the entorhinal cortex and hippocampal CA1 of human AD brains. We have identified several TTBK1 phosphorylation sites that overlap with PHF-tau sites (pTyr197, pSer198, pSer199, pSer202) on full-length human tau (PMID 16923168). Further, TTBK1 directly phosphorylates tau at a pre-tangle marker site (pSer422), as well as one of the AT8 recognition sites (pSer202/pThr205), illustrating its potential role in the modulation of tau pathology in AD.

Here, we employed antisense-oligonucleotide (ASO) technology to specifically target mouse Ttbk1 mRNA in PS19 (TauP301S) tauopathy mice at 6 months of age and evaluated phosphorylated tau (p-tau) levels by ELISA (PMID 37853497), hippocampal AT8+ p-tau accumulation, gliosis and synaptic density via immunofluorescence, neuroinflammation via Olink, spatial transcriptomics via MerSCOPE, and functional phenotypes via the open field test at 8-weeks post-injection.

We observed a significant reduction of AT8+ p-tau in the hippocampus of ASO-treated mice, accompanied by synaptic rescue in the CA1, reduction in cortical atrophy, and reduction of PS19 mouse hypermobility phenotype. ASO administration did not augment neuroinflammation via gliosis in PS19 mice or cytokine increases in WT mice, establishing its safety and tolerability. Spatial transcriptomics revealed a decrease in p-tau-associated OPC-Oligodendrocyte cell population after ASO-Ttbk1 treatment, indicating a new cellular response for disease amelioration.
Together, our study establishes TTBK1 as a disease-modifying driver of tau pathology and support ASO-mediated TTBK1 suppression as a safe, translational therapeutic strategy for AD patients.

affiliations: Division of Endocrinology, Diabetes, and Metabolism, Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, Florida
s2-02.keywords: Obesity, Weight management, GLP-1s, Bariatric Surgery

p: Patients seeking weight management often hold weight-loss expectations exceeding what available interventions offer. How expectations align with patients’ willingness to pursue evidence-based treatments remains poorly described.
To describe weight-loss expectations, treatment preferences, and the alignment between expectations and treatment uptake among patients seeking weight management.

We retrospectively reviewed electronic medical records of adults attending an initial weight management consultation from 2019-2025. Demographics, clinical characteristics, weight-loss goals, and interest in and uptake of dietary support, behavior therapy, obesity medication (OM), endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG), and metabolic bariatric surgery (MBS) were extracted. Analyses included Student’s t-tests, Pearson correlations, and ANOVA.

We included 774 participants (age 51±14 years, 76% female, 91% White, weight 116±27 kg, BMI 41±8 kg/m²); 52% had class III obesity, and 99.5% had ≥1 obesity-related disease. Of 656 (85%) interested in dietary support, 461 (62%) attended ≥1 dietitian visit; of 355 (46%) interested in behavior modification therapy, 179 (24%) attended ≥1 therapy session. Among 750 OM-eligible patients, 571 (74%) expressed interest and were prescribed one including semaglutide (32%), tirzepatide (21%), or phentermine/topiramate (19%). Among ESG- or MBS-eligible patients, 80/383 (21%) and 150/526 (29%) expressed interest, of whom 41 (51%) accepted gastroenterology referral and 89 (59%) surgical referral, respectively. Patients interested in MBS reported higher weight-loss goals than those interested in OM alone or OM+ESG (36±10% vs. 26±10% and 22±7%; p<0.001). Those not interested in any intervention reported goals of 26±12%. One-third of patients reported ≥1 non-weight goal including improvement in health (21.6%), mobility (7.7%), pain (4.8%), and appearance (2.7%).

Patients seeking weight management often set weight-loss goals exceeding realistic outcomes. Despite high initial interest, treatment uptake was substantially lower across all modalities, revealing a gap between interest and engagement. These findings highlight the need to calibrate patient expectations and address barriers to care uptake.

affiliations: Department of Neuroscience, Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, Florida
s2-03.keywords: Alzheimer’s Disease, Tau Propagation, Braak Staging, Humanized Animal Models, Neuronal Excitability

p: In Alzheimer’s disease (AD), phosphorylated tau first appears in entorhinal cortex layer II (ECII) and subsequently spreads to the hippocampus and the cerebral cortex. We developed a mouse model that recapitulates early tau propagation by injecting AAV2/6 expressing Cre-inducible P301L human tau (AAV-FLEX-tauP301L) into ECII of Wolframin1-Cre (Wfs1) mice. In this study, to determine how human tau and amyloid-β influence tau propagation and neuronal excitability, we generated human MAPT knock-in Wfs1 (T-Wfs1) and APPNL-G-F/MAPT double-knock-in Wfs1 (AT-Wfs1) mice.

Wfs1, T-Wfs1, and AT-Wfs1 mice received unilateral ECII injections of AAV-FLEX-tauP301L at 7 months of age and were analyzed 3 months later. Immunohistochemistry assessed human tau (HT7), phosphorylated tau (AT8), misfolded tau (Alz50), Parvalbumin/Somatostatin positive inhibitory (PV+/SST+ IN) and Neurogranin positive excitatory neurons (NRGN+ EN). Field electrophysiology measured spontaneous activity in hippocampal and neocortical regions before and after GABA-A receptor blockade with gabazine. GeoMx Digital Spatial Profiling was performed on PV+IN and NRGN+EN from uninjected 7-month-old Wfs1 and AT-Wfs1 brains.

HT7+ tau reached CA1 and subiculum in Wfs1 mice, whereas AT8+ and Alz50+ tau were absent. In T-Wfs1 mice, HT7+, AT8+, and Alz50+ tau extended to CA1, subiculum, and neocortex and were further increased in AT-Wfs1 mice. Of total AT8+ tau, 34.7% colocalized with NRGN+ EN, whereas <1% colocalized with PV+/SST+ IN, indicating preferential propagation to excitatory neurons. T-Wfs1 and AT-Wfs1 mice showed increased spontaneous firing compared with Wfs1 mice, with little further increase after gabazine, consistent with impaired GABAergic transmission. Both lines also exhibited reduced PV+ IN numbers independent of tau spread. In PV+ IN from AT-Wfs1 mice, genes related to fast-spiking, Ca2+ homeostasis, excitatory recruitment, and synaptic function were selectively downregulated, together with a predicted upstream transcriptional regulator.

Human tau and amyloid pathology cooperatively enhance neuronal hyperexcitability and tau propagation from ECII to hippocampal and neocortical regions, implicating inhibitory circuit dysfunction in early AD. Ongoing studies test whether recipient-cell excitability regulates tau propagation using DREADDs and whether transcriptional regulator agonism can restore E/I balance in AT-Wfs1 mice.

affiliations: Division of Heart Failure and Transplantation, Mayo Clinic, Florida, Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, Florida
s2-04.keywords: lactate, lactic acid clearance, cardiogenic shock, Impella 5.5, heart failure, mechanical circulatory support

p: Lactate clearance is a key biomarker of end-organ perfusion and prognosis in cardiogenic shock, but the optimal assessment window for prognostication after Impella 5.5 implantation remains uncertain. Current studies have shown 24-hour lactic acid levels to haev prognostic value. We aim to re-assess this optimal window of lactate clearance and take this further to show long-term trends by final outcome groups.

We retrospectively evaluated lactate trajectories in cardiogenic shock patients supported with Impella 5.5 between January 2020 and September 2025. We stratified outcomes as those transplanted, recovered, underwent durable LVAD (dLVAD) implantation, or died while supported by Impella 5.5. For survival analysis, transplant, recovery, and dLVAD were grouped as “survivors” and compared with those who died. Logistic regression was used to evaluate mortality risk.

190 patients were included: 153 transplanted, 10 recovered, 13 received dLVAD, and 14 died. Time from admission to Impella implantation and pre-Impella lactate levels did not differ across outcome groups. Pre-Impella lactate levels were not statistically different across the 4 outcome groups.

At 24 hours, lactate levels declined across all outcome groups with minimal separation between survivors and non-survivors. By 72-hours, divergence was evident: survivors demonstrated sustained clearance, while non-survivors had persistent elevation. On univariate analysis, 24-hour lactate was associated with an odds ratio (OR) 1.69 (p=0.11) for mortality, while 72-hour lactate levels showed a stronger association OR 6.04 (p<0.001). On multivariate analysis, 24-hour lactate remained significantly associated with mortality (OR 2.08, p=0.036), and 72-hour lactate demonstrated an even stronger association (OR 15.9, p=0.003).
These findings highlight that 72-hour lactate clearance, not 24-hour, more accurately predicts mortality after Impella 5.5 implantation.

affiliations: Molecular Medicine, Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, Florida
s2-05.keywords: Glioblastoma, Immunotherapy, Metabolism, CAR-T cells, Solid tumors

p: Glioblastoma (GBM) is a highly aggressive and treatment-resistant brain malignancy, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) substantially limits the efficacy of the chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy. A major barrier is metabolic competition within the TME, where highly glycolytic GBM cells consume major glucose and generate nutrient-deprived TME that compromises the T-cell persistence and function. We hypothesize that metabolically reprogramming CAR T-cells to sustain glucose utilization will enhance their fitness and anti-tumor activity in GBM.

CD70 targeted CAR T-cells were genetically engineered to overexpress either glucose transporter- GLUT1 or GLUT3. Metabolic fitness was assessed by LiCellMo-metabolic profiling. Functional activity was evaluated through coculture with GBM cell line under glucose restricted conditions. CAR T-cell activation, target cell avidity, proliferation and cytotoxicity were assessed using ELISA, Cell avidity assay, Flowcytometry analysis and NanoLive live cell imaging. Therapeutic efficacy was further evaluated in immunocompromised orthotopic GBM mouse models by measuring intratumoral CAR T cell presence, tumor burden and overall survival.

Overexpression of GLUT1/3 significantly increased glucose uptake by CD70 CAR T-cells at baseline and following antigen stimulation, demonstrating enhanced metabolic fitness. Metabolically engineered CAR T cells exhibited greater activation and functional capacity compared with control CAR t cells, including increased avidity and increased tumor cell killing specially under glucose restricted conditions that mimic the GBM TME. In vivo, GLUT1/3 overexpressing CAR T-cells demonstrated improved tumor infiltration and persistence within GBM lesions, showing enhanced tumor control and prolonged survival.

Metabolic enhancement of CD70 CAR T-cells through GLUT1/3 overexpression improves glucose utilization, sustains effector function under nutrient stress, and enhances antitumor activity against GBM. These findings demonstrate that immune metabolic reprogramming can overcome key metabolic barriers imposed by GBM TME and support further development of metabolically optimized CAR T-cell therapies as a strategy to improve outcomes for patients with glioblastoma.

s2-06.keywords: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO) Lung Transplantation ,Acute Kidney Injury, Renal Replacement Therapy, Critical Care Outcomes

p: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is increasingly being used as a bridge to transplant (BTT) due to recent changes in lung allocation policy that prioritize critically ill candidates. We present a seven-year, single-center analysis of post-transplant outcomes comparing recipients bridged with ECMO to those transplanted without bridging support.

We performed a retrospective single-center study of adult lung transplant recipients from 2018–2024 using institutional EHR data. Patients were categorized by ECMO support at transplantation (Bridge ECMO vs No Bridge). The groups were compared in terms of baseline characteristics, operative factors, transfusion burden, and postoperative outcomes. Predictors of acute kidney injury (AKI) requiring dialysis for one year were found using multivariable logistic regression. Kaplan-Meier analysis was used to evaluate survival.

Among 319 lung transplant recipients, 36 (11.3%) underwent transplantation while supported with ECMO. Bridged recipients were younger at transplant (58.6 vs 63.2 years, p=0.011) and required significantly higher perioperative transfusion (p<0.001). Postoperative complications were more frequent in the ECMO group, including acute kidney injury (72.2% vs 49.1%, p=0.009), infection/sepsis (27.8% vs 14.1%, p=0.034), and longer ICU stay (54.5 vs 10 days, p<0.001). Dialysis-requiring AKI at one year occurred in 50.0% vs 12.7% (p<0.001).

In multivariable analysis, post-transplant cardiogenic shock (aOR 7.49), serum creatinine at one month (aOR 11.27), and ICU length of stay (per 10 days, aOR 1.48; all p<0.001) independently predicted dialysis-requiring AKI, while ECMO bridging did not (aOR 2.74, p=0.281). One-year mortality (30.6% vs 29.3%, p=0.879) and post-transplant survival (HR 1.42, 95% CI 0.75–2.67) were similar.

ECMO bridging enabled transplantation accessible to selected groups of critically ill patients during this seven-year single-center experience. ECMO bridging was not associated with worse short- or intermediate-term survival, despite being linked to increased perioperative morbidity and resource utilization. This suggests that ECMO bridging is a viable treatment option but requires focused strategies to mitigate renal injury and perioperative morbidity.

s2-07.keywords: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension, Seizures, Epilepsy, Intracranial Pressure, Cohort Study

p: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) is primarily characterized by headache and visual dysfunction, yet accumulating evidence suggests broader neurologic manifestations, including skull base remodeling, temporal encephaloceles, and seizures. Whether IIH is associated with an increased risk of seizures or epilepsy remains uncertain. We evaluated the incidence of seizures or epilepsy after an IIH diagnosis compared with matched individuals without IIH and assessed whether any observed association could be explained by differential ascertainment.

We conducted a retrospective matched cohort study across all three Mayo Clinic sites. Adults with IIH were identified using diagnostic codes supported by lumbar puncture findings or repeated coding, with at least 12 months of pre-index records and follow-up. Patients with prior seizures or epilepsy were excluded. Comparators without IIH were matched on age, sex, and body mass index and were drawn from the same health system. Incident seizure or epilepsy was defined using validated coding criteria and antiseizure medication records. The primary outcome was the 3-year cause-specific hazard ratio, with death treated as a competing risk. A prespecified negative-control framework was used to evaluate potential surveillance bias.

Primary cohort included 2,606 patients with IIH and 4,037 matched comparators (mean age 34.7 years, 87% female, mean BMI 36.3 kg/m²). Seventy-four incident seizure or epilepsy events occurred during follow-up. Incidence rates were 9.38 per 1,000 person-years in the IIH group and 1.78 per 1,000 person-years among comparators. IIH was associated with a significantly increased risk of seizures or epilepsy (hazard ratio 5.58, 95% CI 3.15-9.87, p<0.001). Three-year cumulative incidence was 2.54% versus 0.49%, corresponding to an absolute risk increase of 2.05 percentage points. Negative-control analyses suggested that baseline imbalances and surveillance bias were unlikely to fully explain the observed association.

Patients with IIH exhibited a higher incidence of seizures and epilepsy than matched controls, with approximately a fivefold relative increase in risk. Although causality cannot be established, the findings indicate that seizure risk warrants consideration in the clinical management of IIH and support prospective studies incorporating detailed imaging, cerebrospinal fluid measures, and electroencephalographic confirmation of seizure events.

s2-08.keywords: preoperative assessment, postoperative cardiovascular events, submaximal cardiopulmonary exercise testing, Submaximal Heart and Pulmonary Evaluation (SHAPE) Test, postoperative cardiac risk.

p: Postoperative major adverse cardiac events (MACE) remain a leading cause of perioperative morbidity and mortality. The assessment of cardiovascular risk prediction before elective surgery continues to be challenging for clinicians. The Submaximal Heart and Pulmonary Evaluation (SHAPE) Test is a noninvasive, cardiopulmonary stress test that measures exercise capacity and physiological response to exertion. It is used in the evaluation and management of patients with pulmonary hypertension. However, its role in predicting postoperative cardiovascular complications remains underexplored. This study evaluates whether SHAPE testing, regardless of indication, is associated with the incidence of postoperative MACE at 30, 90 days, and one year following surgery.

We retrospectively identified adult patients with ≥ 18 years of age who underwent elective procedures at a single healthcare system from January 1, 2021, to January 1, 2025. All patients completed a preoperative SHAPE Test within one year before surgery. Postoperative MACE were defined as myocardial infarction, heart failure, stroke, and death within 30, 90 days, and one year following surgery, as measures for the primary endpoint.

A total of 88 patients (median age, 62; 68.2% women; median BMI, 29.6 kg/m2) were included. Postoperative MACE occurred in 12 (13.6%) patients within 1 year postoperatively. The median VO2max from the SHAPE test was 9.8 ml/kg/min (interquartile range, 9.0 – 13.5) among patients who experienced a MACE event, compared with 14.6 ml/kg/min (interquartile range, 12.8 – 16.7) among those who did not. We found an inverse relationship between VO2max and MACE, estimating an approximated 28% reduction in the odds of MACE for each 1 mL/kg/min increase in VO2max (OR 0.73, 95% CI 0.57 – 0.90, p=0.002).

Findings and the analysis suggest that SHAPE Test may improve preoperative clinical risk stratification before an elective noncardiac surgery. Further prospective studies in larger and more diverse populations are needed to support its application to improve surgical outcomes in preoperative care.

s2-09.keywords: Partial nephrectomy, Mayo Adhesive Probability score, Abdominal aortic calcium score, Renal function

p: The Mayo Adhesive Probability (MAP) score estimates adherent perinephric fat and operative difficulty before partial nephrectomy, while abdominal aortic calcium score (AACS) may reflect vascular and renal vulnerability. We examined the complementary value of these computed tomography (CT)-based measures in characterizing operative complexity and renal outcomes.

We retrospectively studied 301 patients who underwent partial nephrectomy. MAP was measured on both kidneys, with MAP ≥3 considered positive; AACS was analyzed continuously and at a cutoff of ≥1000. Operative outcomes included sticky fat and operative time. Renal outcomes included 12-month estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), percent change in eGFR, new-onset chronic kidney disease (CKD) among patients with baseline eGFR ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m², and chronic renal pathology. Multivariable models adjusted for relevant clinical, tumor, and operative factors. An exploratory mediation analysis evaluated whether sticky fat explained the association between MAP and operative time.

Mean age was 61.1±11.6 years, 64.1% were male, mean BMI was 29.9±6.0 kg/m², and mean baseline eGFR was 77.7±20.6 mL/min/1.73 m² (Table 1). AACS remained independently associated with chronic renal pathology (OR 1.17 per log-unit; 95% CI, 1.03–1.32; p=0.014), and AACS ≥1000 was associated with higher odds of chronic renal pathology (OR 2.19; 95% CI, 1.08–4.56; p=0.032). When AACS and bilateral MAP were modeled together, AACS remained associated with lower 12-month eGFR (p=0.029), while MAP was weaker (p=0.063) (Table 2). MAP was strongly associated with sticky fat (OR 3.6 per point; p<0.001) and longer operative time (+5.36 minutes per point; 95% CI, 2.43–8.29; p<0.001). After adjustment for sticky fat, the MAP effect fell by 75% and was no longer significant; sticky fat itself added 21.7 minutes (p=0.002). Mediation analysis showed a significant indirect effect through sticky fat (+5.03 minutes; p<0.001). Neither score was independently associated with new-onset CKD.

MAP and AACS appear to capture different preoperative risk domains. MAP mainly reflects the local operative environment and adherent fat, whereas AACS is more closely linked to chronic renal disease and postoperative renal function. Together, they may provide complementary rather than redundant information before partial nephrectomy.

p: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), including semaglutide and tirzepatide, are widely used for weight management and have shown cardiovascular risk reduction in patients with obesity and type 2 diabetes. However, their effects on cardiac structure and function in patients with obesity and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) remain poorly characterized, and it is unclear whether any benefits are driven by weight loss itself.

A propensity score-matched retrospective cohort study using Mayo Clinic data (2018–2024). Adults with obesity and HFrEF receiving semaglutide or tirzepatide for weight management for at least 12 months (GLP-1+) were matched 1:2 to HFrEF controls without GLP-1 RA exposure (GLP-1−) on age, sex, BMI, type 2 diabetes (exact), and baseline comorbidities (hypertension, atrial fibrillation, CAD, CKD, dyslipidemia, pulmonary hypertension, depression, anxiety, stroke/TIA, hypothyroidism) using nearest-neighbor matching with a 0.25 SD caliper. Echocardiographic parameters were extracted at baseline, year 1, and year 2. Longitudinal changes were evaluated using linear mixed-effects models adjusted for baseline values, comorbidities, and baseline use of guideline-directed medical therapies (ARNI, SGLT-2 inhibitors, MRAs), with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction. Results are reported as between-group differences (95% CI).

We matched 146 GLP-1+ patients to 237 GLP-1− controls; baseline characteristics were similar (mean age 61 vs 62 years; 67.1% vs 72.6% male; BMI 34.3 ± 5.5 vs 34.9 ± 9.0 kg/m²). At year 1, GLP-1+ patients had significantly greater total body weight loss than controls (−5.1 ± 8.6% vs −0.8 ± 7.8%; p<0.001). Compared to controls, GLP-1+ patients showed significantly greater improvements in LV function and remodeling: LV ejection fraction +4.1% (1.4 to 6.8), q=0.016; LV end-diastolic diameter −3.2 mm (−4.8 to −1.6), q=0.001; LV end-systolic diameter −4.0 mm (−6.1 to −2.0), q=0.001; and LV mass index −11.2 g/m² (−17.9 to −4.5), q=0.007; all surviving FDR correction. After additional adjustment for weight change, improvements in LV end-diastolic diameter (q=0.038), LV end-systolic diameter (q=0.024), and LV mass index (q=0.009) remained significant, while the LVEF difference was attenuated (q=0.115). No significant differences were observed in diastolic parameters. Exploratory 2-year analyses showed progressive remodeling with continued improvements in LVEF (+5.9% [2.5 to 9.3]) and LV mass index (−14.6 g/m² [−23.2 to −6.1]).

In patients with obesity and HFrEF, semaglutide or tirzepatide was associated with significant improvements in LV systolic function and reverse remodeling over 1–2 years versus matched controls. Structural remodeling persisted after adjustment for weight loss and background GDMT, suggesting partially weight-independent cardioprotective effects, while the LVEF improvement was attenuated after accounting for weight change.

s2-11.keywords: Cancer Clinical Trials; Health Communication; Artificial Intelligence; Patient Education; Patient-Provider Communication

p: Facilitating patients’ ability to ask informed questions about clinical trials is a component of ethical recruitment and informed consent. Clear and accessible trial information can help patients and families understand complex concepts, prepare for communication with research teams, and build confidence to ask relevant questions. ALEX (Agents Leveraging Empathy for EXams) is an AI-enabled cancer clinical trial portal. We examined what questions participants identified during ALEX, their plans for follow-up, and whether participants could find ALEX easy to understand while also wanting additional communication.

We used a mixed-methods analysis of data from 136 adults across four sites (Mayo Clinic Jacksonville/UF Gainesville/UF Jacksonville/University of Miami). From November 2023 to April 2025, we conducted 34 focus group or think-aloud sessions. Participants completed pre/post questionnaires. Transcripts were coded by thought unit, a discrete participant utterance connecting a question or information need to a next step. Spearman correlations examined one ease-of-understanding item and three motivation items, with Holm adjustment.

Perceived ease of understanding was positively associated with motivation to learn more, discuss clinical research with a doctor, and discuss with people who help make health care decisions (ρ=.308-.402, all Holm-adjusted p<.001). 89.3% found ALEX easy to understand, 87.8% wanted to learn more, 75.6% wanted to talk to a doctor, and 74.8% wanted to talk to those who help make health care decisions. Across 22 sessions, 34 thought units were identified. Question preparation was the most frequent communication strategy (n=12), followed by clarification (n=10). Participants identified questions about source credibility, personal relevance, study requirements, and safety. For follow-up, health care providers were identified in 13 thought units and research staff in 11. Participants described ALEX as useful for helping them formulate questions and identify sources of information.

Participants found ALEX easy to understand and reported motivation for further information seeking about clinical trials. Qualitative findings suggest that ALEX may support patients and families in preparing questions and identifying sources for follow-up. By facilitating question preparation and communication, ALEX may enhance the quality of patient-provider communication around cancer clinical trials.
